title_original: Downtown, Behind the Scenes of the City

blocks.text: Armed with his film Leica, Alexis Duclos roams the city in search of the unexpected. Where his first exhibition, “En Ville” (“In the City”), captured the poetry of Parisian streets, “Downtown” extends his gaze to other horizons. He builds a monochrome series with a vibrant grain, in which black and white contrasts make light the guiding thread of this urban wandering. The sun rises and floods a Parisian facade, blazes over a Tokyo boulevard at its zenith, then its last rays timidly caress a New York building: across 20 photographs, the exhibition itself becomes a wandering that mirrors the photographer’s own.

We move from one metropolis to another without transition, carried by the same invisible thread linking streets across the world. In the end, it hardly matters where an image was taken, since the city rocks us with the same refrain, as if all cities shared a common language that only the eye could reveal.

From the cover image on, Alexis Duclos shows us that the monumental city and ordinary bodies share the same sky. A knee bent like an arch, a hand wrapped around it. Below, a row of curved backs, bare shoulders, legs dangling at the water’s edge, and far in the background, tiny, almost shy, the iron lady watching over Paris. In this oversized foreground, where flesh becomes landscape, we are plunged into the almost indecent intimacy of the framing.

The photographer plays with dimensions, shifting scales, inviting us to look differently. The fairground is transformed into a Hollywood spectacle, where a papier-mâché King Kong, turned silent guardian of a carousel, looms above the crowd, jaws open on a silent roar, reaching an arm toward the sky as if to pluck the silhouettes spinning at the end of their metal cables.

Nothing is ever quite what it seems, and facades sometimes turn into backstage. That is the case with this image, titled Ascension, where the giant shadow of a service staircase unfolds across a metal fence. We see only the staircase’s reflection, a ghostly, projected version, theatrically lit. As if the building were watching itself, and the cast shadow were the only stage where the real spectacle could finally play out. A set worthy of theater or cinema, it is impossible not to think of The Truman Show. One almost expects to see the character, mid-ascent, reach the top, turn to the audience, take one last bow, and deliver a final line: “Good morning, good afternoon, and good night.”
Film photography, a return to the source

For more than twenty years, Alexis Duclos worked at the heart of current events. Starting in 1985, after a stint at Associated Press, he joined the Gamma agency, where he covered conflicts, political news, sports, and major international events. A photographer honored with several awards, he developed a practice marked by the diversity of terrain he explored. In 2005, as photojournalism underwent major upheaval, he decided to leave Gamma to devote himself to independent projects, moving between documentary photography and audiovisual production. Then, over the years, he gradually turned away from reportage to rediscover the simple pleasure of a photography freed from economic and editorial constraints.

Like a flâneur, Alexis Duclos lets himself be guided by chance. He moves forward with no apparent itinerary, attentive to what escapes hurried eyes. For him, photographing means learning to see, frame, and release the shutter at the right moment. His photographic style is distinctive, built on a rigorous composition in which every element finds its place and contributes to the image’s meaning. “I compose with light and framing to express a moment that, I hope, provokes emotions. That’s when a photograph can speak to me, can speak to us. Or not. It’s simple and complex at once.”

The only constraint the photographer imposes on himself is his choice of focal length: a 50mm lens, the one whose rendering comes closest to human eye perception. Alexis Duclos works exclusively on film: “I love black and white film for its grain, its texture, its material quality, and its aesthetic.” In his view, unlike digital photography and artificial intelligence, where images can be recomposed or artificially generated, film embodies a return to a photographic practice grounded in the materiality of the negative, an indisputable sign that a moment truly existed.

Here, implicitly, we find Roland Barthes’s intuition about photography’s indexical power: the image as trace, as proof that something truly was there, in front of the lens, in a light and an instant that will never occur again.
“Downtown,” by Alexis Duclos, is on view at La Caverne D’Art & Miss gallery in Paris, from September 24 to October 24, 2026.
